candidates.source_name: Ephrem the Syrian / Commentary on Genesis
candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis IX.13 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 362 AD)

On the rainbow as covenantal sign — 'I do set my bow (qashti) in the cloud' — Ephrem makes the most of the Hebrew qesheth's dual sense of 'bow' = both rainbow AND warrior's weapon. God sets His bow (war-weapon) in the cloud: His instrument of judgment is permanently sheathed as covenantal pledge that the universal-deluge mode of judgment will not recur. The bow is set with its string facing downward (toward earth) and its arc facing upward — figuratively, the weapon is laid aside, not aimed. Ephrem reads this as the textual root of the Syriac patristic teaching that divine wrath, while real, is never the final word: the rainbow stands over every subsequent storm as the visible reminder that mercy has the last word.

candidates.source_name: Ephrem the Syrian / Commentary on Genesis
candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis IX.25 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 362 AD)

Noah's pronouncement after the Ham-incident — 'Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be unto his brethren' — Ephrem reads with careful precision against any reading that would extract a permanent racial-ethnic curse. The curse falls on CANAAN (Ham's son), not on Ham himself or on Ham's other descendants; the cursing is therefore localized and historical (fulfilled in the Canaanite-Israelite encounters of Joshua-Judges), not racially universal. Against the early-modern American mis-application of this verse to justify African slavery, Ephrem's text-bounded reading clearly precludes such extension: the curse is on a specific lineage (Canaan), for a specific reason (Canaan's prefigured idolatry and immorality), with a specific fulfillment (the dispossession of the Canaanite peoples by Israel). The Tewahedo reading inherits Ephrem's text-bounded precision.

candidates.source_name: Ephrem the Syrian / Commentary on Genesis
candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis IX.13 (NPNF S2 V13). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 362 AD)

On the rainbow as covenantal sign — 'I do set my bow (qashti) in the cloud' — Ephrem makes the most of the Hebrew qesheth's dual sense of 'bow' = both rainbow AND warrior's weapon. God sets His bow (war-weapon) in the cloud: His instrument of judgment is permanently sheathed as covenantal pledge that the universal-deluge mode of judgment will not recur. The bow is set with its string facing downward (toward earth) and its arc facing upward — figuratively, the weapon is laid aside, not aimed. Ephrem reads this as the textual root of the Syriac patristic teaching that divine wrath, while real, is never the final word: the rainbow stands over every subsequent storm as the visible reminder that mercy has the last word.
